At low temperatures, the electronic systems of two-dimensional materials, such as quantum wells and monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides, become predominantly hole or electron holes, making it feasible through experiment or theory to determine the non-thermal Fermi energy ($E_F$) via the thermopower (Seebeck coefficient), defined as $S = -\pi k_B/3e(E_F/T)$. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of MaskedSpeech in producing situational outputs that adhere to these masking laws and in facilitating better listener comprehension, thereby improving overall communication quality.

Nuclear migration along the retinal thickness, termed "interkinetic nuclear movement" (IKNM), outlines a fundamental stage of neuroretina development. During this process, nuclei reach the apical surface during the G1 phase of the cell cycle, move to the basal surface by the G1/S transition, remain there through S and G2 phases, and return to the apex during mitosis. Although the discrete steps of cell division drive retinal tissue expansion and neuroretina maturation, questions persist regarding the regulatory mechanisms governing movement between cellular cycles. By utilizing live zebrafish embryos, we tracked these nuclei in real time and analyzed the associated transitions of cell division. Our computational findings suggest that diffusive motion accounts for IKNM. We utilized this diffusion principle to create a numerical model incorporating distinct coefficients for each region, which accurately reproduces the observed trajectory and displacement of the nuclei.

The metric dimension of a graph $G$ (denated as $\dim(G)$) is defined as the size of the resolving set with the fewest elements possible. Any such set $W \subseteq V(G)$ that minimizes cardinality must identify distinct vertices by comparing their metric distances to at least one member of $W$. This dimension refers to the metric dimension associated with $\tau$-resolving sets. Specifically, a subset $W$ qualifies as a $\tau$-resolving set if, for every graph vertex $u$, the distance to $W$ differs from that of any other distinct vertex $v$ by a factor strictly less than $1-\tau$; that is, either $\frac{d(u,v)}{\min \{d(w,u):w \in W\}} < 1+\tau$ or $\frac{d(u,v)}{\max \{d(w,u):w \in W\}} < 1+\tau$. If no such subset $W$ exists, then $dim_t(G,\tau)=+\infty$. We explore various properties related to this dimension, how it connects to the standard metric dimension, and examine specific determination of its value or tight upper bounds for several standard families of graphs.

Motion deinterlacing involves reconstructing full-frame images from half-resolution, interlaced signals by generating the missing scanfield. Although essential for maintaining high-quality moving image display, many existing solutions are unsuitable for modern systems because they either fail to process the input in real-time or compromise image quality. This paper presents a new approach, DeepMotionDeinterlacing (DDI), a deep learning model designed to handle 60Hz progressive displays. The system uses a 2-to-1 overscan strategy that captures one scanfield per 60ms interval; when the second field arrives, a sliding window technique applies the DDI network to produce a real-time full-frame output with updates every 30ms. For implementation, the DDI network leverages the powerful Esrgan architecture enhanced by motion information (EXGM) to improve movement prediction accuracy. A training dataset, MotionWebDF, was built by assigning labels to massive collections of video clips and then overlaying the captured sliding windows. After training, tests show that DDI delivers superior results for both subjective evaluation and objective metrics compared to top-tier baseline methods, with all operations running efficiently in the PyTorch framework.

Precise theoretical prediction of fundamental and exotic neutron distribution root-mean-square (rms) radii remains essential for characterizing nuclear and astrophysical systems, including those involved in neutron stars. Accurately predicting river flow velocities and water elevations is vital for forecasting natural disasters, managing aquatic ecosystems handling flow contaminants. This confirms the tool's validity and suggests it could be significantly contribute to real-time operations requiring vital flow forecasting.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging a set of exposures taken at varying levels. Training neural networks trained on adequate data often yields complex, non-identifiable mappings that yield equal accuracy but offer differing interpretability, a problem exacerbated in case with insufficient datasets. The study concludes that testing on both retinotopy and epidemiology cases shows reformulating models or adding auxillary variables under NCL realigns learned retinotopy and boosts robustness against distributional shifts.

Process mining has evolved into a significant technique for analyzing business processes by leveraging event logs. One-dimensional optical quasicrystals consist of periodic layers where the thickness of repeated motifs follows an aperiodic but recognizable sequence known as a unique cut-and-project sequence. These structures generate an intricate interference pattern that creates gaps within a photonic band structure. When disorder is introduced by randomly perturbing the thickness of these layers while preserving their average periodicity, two key phenomena emerge: a transition from linear to nonlinear behavior in the interference within the band gap, along with a shift in the delocalization symmetry. Notably, this shift resembles that seen in disordered 1D Anderson systems, yet a key distinction remains; unlike 1D Anderson localization which is entirely linear, quasicrystalline systems exhibit both linear and nonlinear components due to the presence of a superposition interference term. Consequently, by tuning the Anderson transition with appropriate materials and geometric arrangements, it is possible to achieve a shift in the delocalization boundary that experiences no linear component, referring to it as a "reentrant delocalization shift." This study further analyzes the physical mechanisms behind this transition via finite supercell simulations and validates them experimentally with measurements on actual fabricated samples using the same design parameters.

Disruptive events in population dynamics, often termed population cycles or catastrophes, frequently precede unpredictable yet pivotal shifts in ecosystem functioning and biodiversity. Because these events are difficult to foresee, it is essential to identify associated early warning signals (EWS). As a system approaches a regime shift, theorists posit that fluctuations increase in amplitude across multiple timescales; however, quantifying these signals quantitatively remains difficult due to data requirements across frequency spectrums. Addressing the limitation of needing extensive time-series data, we utilize a theoretical two-timescale model of ecosystem competition to quantify increases in amplitude within the model itself as warning indicators. Specifically, we determine amplitude thresholds corresponding to abrupt transitions in one timescale dynamics resulting in long-term ecosystem shifts. Our results indicate that amplitude augmentation constitutes a viable precursor to regime shifts; we define the specific threshold values that differentiate transient dynamics from persistent, non-transient transients. Furthermore, we observe slowed oscillatory crossings near bifurcation points, suggesting that amplitude increase may precede such transitions, although distinct threshold levels are necessary to reliably predict non-transient outcomes over the long term.

Parkinson's Disease represents the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide and is characterized by the degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons within the substantia nigra of the brain's basal ganglia circuitry. Our simulations target two primary mechanisms of PD: (i) PD induced by the selective elimination of dopamine neurons, primarily within the substantia nigra pars compacta, and (ii) PD resulting in local local connectivity modifications associated with neuron loss. By integrating structural parameters and a physiological learning algorithm, the model achieves a precise separation of normal activity from PD-related outcomes, offering a novel theoretical architecture that can guide and enhance future PD research.

Dialog State Tracking (DST) aims to summarize a dialogue's layout at each turn by predicting the user's intentions and inventory of items. Nevertheless, noisy labels prevalent in mainstream datasets markedly impair model performance at this stage. Although previous attempts have addressed these label noise challenges during pre-training on noisy data before fine-tuning, those methods fail to handle noise effectively within the dialogue-specific domains of the target DST task. Observing that DST tasks present a dual-input structure comprising both dialogue histories and individual label components of intents and session-item sets, we note that such noise can be mitigated at training time by leveraging all available audio tracks associated with the dialogue. Human evaluations and benchmark results on the Joint Intent Detection and Slot Filling (JDFF) dataset indicate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with improvements of up to 6.3% and 3.1% in intent prediction and slot filling accuracy, respectively, compared to the best prior results.

We introduce an extension to the basic modal $\mu$-calculus called the version with "entities," which adds a distinct kind of variable referring either to individual states or subsets of states that always include the current state. This addition allows the logic to express properties regarding reachability and separation that were missing from the original framework. Furthermore, we prove computational complexity results for both the original logic and the new extension; specifically, the original logic remains PSPACE-complete, while the proposed logic with entities becomes undecidable. Finally, we provide a translation from the original logic into Linear Temporal Logic with Past and a new framework of "Linear Temporal Logic with Past and Unbounded Past," analyzing the complexity bounds for the resulting framework.

A classic problem originating from the work of Broersama, Broersama, and Wind asks for the initial level $g$ at which a simple graph possesses a signed graph double cover. In this paper, we introduce the notion of expanded generalised signed graph double covers, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for their existence. We provide examples demonstrating that an expanded generalised signed graph double cover may exist at a level lower than any of its standard variants. Under specific conditions, we demonstrate that the critical expanded generalised signed graph double cover always exists for cycle graphs and their standard generalized versions. Additionally, we offer bounds for the critical parameter of this index for any graph order up to $10!$. Finally, we establish several properties associated with this index and its corresponding bound.

This study derives representations in phase space for Weyl-Wigner operators and functions concerning a single bosonic mode, specifically for Wick-ordered powers of creation and annihilator operators. A general thermal equilibrium state at temperature $T$ is then characterized by determining the mean value of these functions under this statistical equilibrium. Consequently, closed-form expressions are achieved for the Weyl distribution and Wigner function of a Wick-ordered thermal state. The paper concludes demonstrating that both the matrix elements of the thermal state itself, when expressed in Fock basis, and its corresponding Weyl distribution exhibit Gaussian behavior as functions of phase space coordinates.

Negative absolute temperatures are indeed counterintuitive, yet they occur in real systems and have been experimentally confirmed. They represent a resource that demands further exploration to fully comprehend their significance. While some aspects of their strange behavior trace back to non-equilibrium conditions or definitions that are not strictly applicable, the fundamental oddities persist even for systems in true thermal equilibrium. Finally, these unique states provide a fertile arena for delving into statistical and thermodynamic concepts with fresh insight.

Although surgical removal remains the primary method for eliminating colorectal cancer, it is crucial to detect and remove colorectal polyps, as these precursors can develop into cancer. Single-pathologist assessment of these specimens can introduce subjective variability, while automated systems offer a means to reduce false positives and false negatives, potentially streamlining clinical workflows and enhancing overall efficacy. Nevertheless, advancing such automation requires access to high-quality datasets. Therefore, we introduce UniToPatho a resource comprising 1,382 histological images of colorectal polyps, annotated by two pathologists with distinct roles: one provided the primary labels (adeno-carcoma grade or normal condition), while the second offered support labels. Furthermore, we offer several task-specific classification models trained on these annotations to accelerate clinical workflows.

We introduce a novel numerical method designed to solve scattering problems featuring smooth coefficient gradients. By applying a coordinate transformation, the problem is mapped onto a computational domain with a unit geometry, which simplifies the original variable coefficients into constant ones. Consequently, standard finite element techniques can be effectively employed, yielding a discrete solution for the transformed problem. Our framework specifically addresses plane wave illumination and scattering by an infinite cylinder oriented perpendicular to the wave's propagation direction, addressing constraints on coefficient derivative magnitudes within the physical domain. A key component of our strategy involves defining discrete mesh adaptation criteria, which are essential for efficiently simulating scattering across various cross-sectional widths. We establish rigorous bounds for these adaptation indicators, demonstrating their capacity to encompass smooth coefficient variations, a result that has been confirmed through numerical experiments.

We calculate general electromagnetic multipoles using bi-vector bases composed of electromagnetic plane wave dipoles. In this representation clear physical meaning is retained, and knowing how to interpret each contribution allows us to simply expand plane wave dipole moments beyond the short wavelength approximation while preserving the interpretation. This approach is useful for understanding each component and permits us to rigorously follow its behavior up to and including higher-order terms. Finally, we apply this formulation to determine electromagnetic forces acting on arbitrary shapes. Traditional force calculations associate rays with multipoles, implying that at short wavelengths only higher-order multipoles interact with them since plane wave dipole meanings are neglected. However, our results demonstrate that, up to and including intermediate orders, plane wave dipole contributions remain physically meaningful; thus we must include lower-order multipoles in addition to the highest ones during the calculation at these scales to accurately represent them.

This paper introduces two new families of homogeneous homogeneous polynomial multi-linear forms, specifically those known as quantum immanants and double Young-Capelli bitableaux, which possess significant applications in quantum group theory and related research fields. We have also explored various connections between these forms and Schur shifted symmetric expressions defined on polynomial rings.

We examine the capability of a specific variant of the scoto-seesaw model to satisfy both the dark matter WIMP abundance and the neutrino mass scaling, alongside its potential to stabilize the Higgs sector. We demonstrate that, even within this minimal minimal extension, there exists a viable parameter space meeting all dark matter relic density constraints in addition to phenomenological requirements for neutrino masses and physical stability. Additionally, we analyze the stability of the model using multiple established methods within the context of these dark matter constraints. Additionally, we explore potential signatures detectable by future $e^+e^-$ colliders for particles located just beyond reach of current experiments.

We examine how birationally induced transformations alter a projective variety's quantum geometry. Under the assumption that the source projective variety possesses ample canonical classes, it is proven that the projective targets of such mappings also hold for ample canonical classes. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Gromov-Witten invariants of the projective target are expressible in terms of those of the source.

Utilizing Chest X-ray (CxR) imaging for diagnostic purposes and monitoring patient conditions is vital, yet enhancing these outcomes often necessitates corresponding improvements in the depicted anatomy. While current methods for refining X-ray imagery exist, they fail to consider clinical context, allowing users to improve visual quality without potentially altering pathological features. We introduce *Illness* - a specialized framework for the context-clinical modification of CXR to address this omission. Its applications span a broad range of scenarios, including procedural support for radiologists, virtual testing of intervention strategies, and the development of enhanced realism in synthetic examples. Its broad utility across diverse cases requires contextual knowledge; therefore, Illness incorporates radiological expertise to generate therapy images that reflect clinically appropriate modifications. Its applications include the training of artificial intelligence models, virtual interventional support, and enhanced therapeutic monitoring for patients.

Developing intuitive tools for the nonlinear visualization and expert analysis of multidimensional vectorial (mdv) data remains notoriously difficult. To enhance existing approaches, we introduce ViDaExpert—a new interactive framework designed to reveal intrinsic structures within deformed 3D volumes. The core of our solution is the integration of a depth buffer technique that effectively renders depth-stitched points in 3D space, avoiding traditional projection methods in complex volumes. By combining these 3D views with 2D slices in an overlapping arrangement, we create an information-rich, clutter-free display layout. Moreover, we offer users control over both view orientation and component importance through interactive "importance maps." Various experimental results analyze real and synthetic datasets, demonstrating the system's efficiency and versatility.
